notes.front: What is gross income, the figure used to decide whether you must file a federal return?
notes.back: All income you receive as money, goods, property and services that isn’t exempt from tax, including income from outside the United States.
notes.explanation: The note under Table 1 adds that income from selling your main home counts even if you can exclude part or all of it.
notes.example: Like adding up wages, bank interest and the value of goods received as pay, but leaving out income that is exempt from tax.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1. 2025 Filing Requirements Chart for Most Taxpayers”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Gross income means all income you receive in the form of money, goods, property, and services that isn’t exempt from tax, including any income from sources outside the United States or from the sale of your main home (even if you can exclude part or all of it).

notes.front: What is filing status, and what does it mainly depend on?
notes.back: The category you file your return under. It depends mainly on whether you are considered unmarried or married.
notes.explanation: Where more than one filing status fits you, Publication 501 says to choose the one that gives the lowest tax.
notes.example: Like choosing which column of the Tax Table to use: a widowed parent may fit two statuses and picks the cheaper one.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Filing Status; Marital Status”, p. 6
notes.evidence: If more than one filing status applies to you, choose the one that will give you the lowest tax. Marital Status In general, your filing status depends on whether you are considered unmarried or married.

notes.front: What is the married filing jointly (MFJ) filing status?
notes.back: Married filing jointly (MFJ): a married couple who both agree to file one return reporting their combined income and allowable expenses.
notes.explanation: Both spouses must agree; one spouse cannot choose a joint return alone.
notes.example: Like a couple pooling two Forms W-2 onto one Form 1040, both signing it.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Married Filing Jointly”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You can choose married filing jointly as your filing status if you are considered married and both you and your spouse agree to file a joint return. On a joint return, you and your spouse report your combined income and deduct your combined allowable expenses.

notes.front: What is the married filing separately (MFS) filing status?
notes.back: Married filing separately (MFS): a married person files their own return, reporting their own income.
notes.explanation: Publication 501 says it may suit someone who wants to be responsible only for their own tax, or when it gives less tax than a joint return.
notes.example: Like two spouses each filing their own Form 1040, each checking the “Married filing separately” box.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Married Filing Separately”, p. 7
notes.evidence: You can choose married filing separately as your filing status if you are married. This filing status may benefit you if you want to be responsible only for your own tax or if it results in less tax than filing a joint return.

notes.front: What is the head of household (HOH) filing status, in one line?
notes.back: Head of household (HOH): a status for someone unmarried or considered unmarried at year end who keeps up a home for a qualifying person.
notes.explanation: All the listed requirements must be met; being unmarried on the last day of the year is only the first of them.
notes.example: Like a single parent who pays for the family flat where their child lives, but only if every test is met.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Head of Household”, p. 8
notes.evidence: You may be able to file as head of household if you meet all the following requirements. 1. You are unmarried or considered unmarried on the last day of the year.

notes.front: What is the qualifying surviving spouse (QSS) filing status?
notes.back: Qualifying surviving spouse (QSS): a status a widowed taxpayer may use for the 2 years after the year their spouse died.
notes.explanation: For the year of death itself, the survivor can instead file jointly with the deceased spouse if otherwise eligible.
notes.example: Like a widower whose wife died in 2024 using this status for 2025 and 2026, but only if the other tests are met.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse”, p. 10
notes.evidence: You may be eligible to use qualifying surviving spouse as your filing status for 2 years following the year your spouse died.

notes.front: What makes a child your qualifying child?
notes.back: The child meets five tests for you: relationship, age, residency, support and joint return.
notes.explanation: A child can pass all five tests for more than one person at once, which is when the tiebreaker rules apply.
notes.example: Like your 12-year-old son who lives with you and does not support himself, but a cousin would fail the relationship test.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Tiebreaker rules”, p. 15
notes.evidence: Sometimes, a child meets the relationship, age, residency, support, and joint return tests to be a qualifying child of more than one person.

notes.front: What is a qualifying relative, in outline?
notes.back: Someone who is nobody’s qualifying child and is either a listed relative or lives with you all year, among other tests.
notes.explanation: The first test rules out anyone who is your, or any other taxpayer’s, qualifying child; gross income and support tests follow.
notes.example: Like a widowed father you support who lives in his own flat, but not a child who is already someone’s qualifying child.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Overview of the Rules for Claiming a Dependent”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative 1. The person can’t be your qualifying child or the qualifying child of any other taxpayer. 2. The person either (a) must be related to you in one of the ways listed under Relatives who don’t have to live with you, or (b) must live with you all year

notes.front: In federal tax, who can be a dependent?
notes.back: Only a person who is either your qualifying child or your qualifying relative.
notes.explanation: Each of the two categories has its own set of tests, covered on the following cards.
notes.example: Like a teenage daughter (a possible qualifying child) or an elderly uncle you support (a possible qualifying relative).
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Dependents The term “dependent” means: • A qualifying child, or • A qualifying relative.

notes.front: What is the green card test?
notes.back: A non-citizen is a tax resident if they were a lawful permanent resident of the United States at any time in the calendar year.
notes.explanation: One day of lawful permanent resident status in 2025 is enough; Publication 519 adds dual-status rules for part-year cases.
notes.example: Like someone issued a Form I-551 Permanent Resident Card in November 2025: they meet the test for 2025.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Green Card Test”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You are a resident for tax purposes if you are a lawful permanent resident of the United States at any time during calendar year 2025. (However, see Dual-Status Aliens, later.) This is known as the green card test.

notes.front: What is the substantial presence test, in outline?
notes.back: A day-count test: physical presence in the United States on at least 31 days this year and 183 weighted days over three years.
notes.explanation: The three-year count covers 2025, 2024 and 2023, with earlier years counted only in part.
notes.example: Like a visiting researcher on a work visa counting their U.S. days, but a green card holder need not count at all.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Substantial Presence Test”, p. 5
notes.evidence: To meet this test, you must be physically present in the United States on at least: 1. 31 days during 2025; and 2. 183 days during the 3-year period that includes 2025, 2024, and 2023, counting:

notes.front: Who is a resident alien for income tax purposes?
notes.back: A non-citizen who meets either the green card test or the substantial presence test for the calendar year.
notes.explanation: Meeting either test is enough; a non-citizen who meets neither may still, in some cases, choose resident treatment for part of the year.
notes.example: Like a foreign engineer in the United States for most of 2025 on a work visa, but not a tourist here for two weeks.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Resident Aliens”, p. 4
notes.evidence: purposes if you meet either the green card test or the substantial presence test for calendar year 2025 (January 1–December 31). Even if you do not meet either of these tests, you may be able to choose to be treated as a U.S. resident for part of the year.

notes.front: Who is a nonresident alien?
notes.back: A non-citizen who meets neither the green card test nor the substantial presence test.
notes.explanation: Nonresident is the starting point: a non-citizen is treated as one unless one of the two residency tests is met.
notes.example: Like a Canadian consultant who visits for 20 days in 2025 and has no green card.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Nonresident Aliens”, p. 4
notes.evidence: If you are an alien (not a U.S. citizen), you are considered a nonresident alien unless you meet one of the two tests described under Resident Aliens below.

notes.front: What is an individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN), and who needs one?
notes.back: Individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN): the IRS number for someone who has no social security number (SSN) and cannot get one.
notes.explanation: An ITIN stands in for the SSN on returns; anyone eligible for an SSN must use that instead.
notes.example: Like a nonresident alien spouse with U.S. rental income and no SSN, but not a green card holder who can get an SSN.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Identification Number”, p. 35
notes.evidence: If you do not have and are not eligible to get an SSN, you must apply for an individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN).

notes.front: What is an Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN), and where does it go on Form 1040?
notes.back: Identity Protection PIN (IP PIN): a six-digit number from the IRS, entered in the IP PIN spaces next to your occupation.
notes.explanation: Only a taxpayer who received an IP PIN enters one; otherwise the spaces stay blank.
notes.example: Like a one-year password on your return: a preparer asks the client for it before e-filing.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Identity Protection PIN”, p. 66
notes.evidence: If you received an IP PIN from the IRS, enter it in the IP PIN spaces provided next to the space for your occupation. You must correctly enter all six numbers of your IP PIN. If you didn’t receive an IP PIN, leave these spaces blank.

notes.front: What is unearned income? Give three examples.
notes.back: Income not earned by working, such as taxable interest, ordinary dividends and capital gain distributions, among others.
notes.explanation: The table also counts unemployment compensation, taxable social security benefits, pensions, annuities and trust distributions of unearned income as unearned.
notes.example: Like interest on a savings account in a child’s name, but not the child’s wages from a summer job.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Table 1-2. 2025 Filing Requirements for Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: In this table, unearned income includes taxable interest, ordinary dividends, and capital gain distributions. It also includes unemployment compensation, taxable social security benefits, pensions, annuities, and distributions of unearned income from a trust.

notes.front: What is the kiddie tax, and on which form is it figured?
notes.back: The tax for certain children who have unearned income, figured on Form 8615 and attached only to the child’s own return.
notes.explanation: The exam’s content outline lists it as minor children’s unearned income (“Kiddie” tax); the form goes with the child’s own Form 1040, not the parent’s.
notes.example: Like a 10-year-old with a large savings account whose return includes Form 8615, but not a child with only wages.
notes.source: Form 8615 (2025), Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income, “Form heading”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income Department of the Treasury Internal Revenue Service Attach only to the child’s Form 1040 or 1040-NR.

notes.front: For the premium tax credit, what is household income?
notes.back: Modified AGI of you and your spouse (if filing jointly), plus that of each dependent who is required to file a return.
notes.explanation: A dependent’s modified AGI is added only when their income meets the filing threshold, so a low-earning child’s income is left out.
notes.example: Like a couple adding their teenager’s pay to their own, but only if the teenager had to file.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit (PTC), “Household income”, p. 4
notes.evidence: household income is the modified adjusted gross income (modified AGI) of you and your spouse (if filing a joint return) (see Line 2a in the Form 8962 instructions) plus the modified AGI of each individual whom you claim as a dependent and who is required to file an income tax return

notes.front: You sit Part 1 in October 2026. A question asks about “the current tax year” and does not name a year. Which law do you apply?
notes.back: C: tax year 2025 law, as amended through 31 December 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Whatever law applies on the exam date
B) Tax year 2026 law
C) Tax year 2025 law, as amended through 31 December 2025
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: for the July 2026 to February 2027 window the bulletin fixes the tested year as calendar 2025 and tells candidates to ignore later changes.
notes.explanation: The candidate bulletin says questions relate to calendar year 2025 unless stated, and that later legislation, court decisions and penalty amounts are out of scope.
notes.source: IRS Special Enrollment Examination Candidate Information Bulletin (PSI, revised August 28, 2026), “Examination content”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: The 2025 Form 1040 must be filed by {{c1::April 15, 2026}}.
notes.explanation: Publication 17 states this date in its What’s New section and points to chapter 1 for more detail.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Due date of return”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Due date of return. File Form 1040 or 1040-SR by April 15, 2026.

notes.front: In March 2026 a new client asks when her 2025 Form 1040 is due. What do you tell her?
notes.back: A: by April 15, 2026.
notes.choices:
A) By April 15, 2026
B) By December 31, 2025
C) By April 15, 2027
notes.choicesExplained: B is the end of the tax year itself, before the return can be complete. C is a year late: that is the due date one year on.
notes.explanation: Publication 17 gives April 15, 2026 as the date to file the 2025 Form 1040.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “What’s New: Due date of return”, p. 3
notes.evidence: File Form 1040 or 1040-SR by April 15, 2026.

notes.front: For 2025, a single taxpayer under 65 must file a return if gross income was at least {{c1::$15,750}}.
notes.explanation: Table 1 sets a gross income floor for each filing status and age; at 65 or older the single figure rises to $17,750.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1. 2025 Filing Requirements Chart for Most Taxpayers”, p. 2
notes.evidence: single under 65 $15,750 65 or older $17,750

notes.front: For 2025, a married couple filing jointly, both under 65, must file if gross income was at least {{c1::$31,500}}.
notes.explanation: The joint figure rises to $33,100 if one spouse is 65 or older and $34,700 if both are.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1. 2025 Filing Requirements Chart for Most Taxpayers”, p. 2
notes.evidence: married filing jointly*** under 65 (both spouses) $31,500 65 or older (one spouse) $33,100 65 or older (both spouses) $34,700

notes.front: For 2025, a taxpayer filing as married filing separately, at any age, must file if gross income was at least {{c1::$5}}.
notes.explanation: Table 1 gives married filing separately one tiny threshold for every age, unlike every other status.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1. 2025 Filing Requirements Chart for Most Taxpayers”, p. 2
notes.evidence: married filing separately any age $5

notes.front: For the Table 1 filing test, when do social security benefits count in gross income? Name both cases.
notes.back: MFS filers who lived with their spouse at any time in 2025; or when half the benefits plus other income exceeds $25,000 ($32,000 MFJ).
notes.explanation: The “other income” in the second case is other gross income plus any tax-exempt interest.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1, footnote on gross income”, p. 2
notes.evidence: Don’t include any social security benefits unless (a) you’re married filing a separate return and you lived with your spouse at any time during 2025, or (b) one-half of your social security benefits plus your other gross income and any tax-exempt interest is more than $25,000 ($32,000 if married filing jointly).

notes.front: Marco, single and 34, had $15,200 of wages in 2025 and no other income. Nobody can claim him as a dependent. Does Table 1’s gross income test require him to file?
notes.back: C: no, $15,200 is below the $15,750 threshold.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the threshold for single filers is $5
B) Yes: every wage earner must file
C) No: $15,200 is below the $15,750 single, under-65 threshold
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: filing depends on the threshold, not on having wages. C confuses single with married filing separately, whose threshold is $5.
notes.explanation: Step by step: single, under 65 → threshold $15,750; his gross income is $15,200; $15,200 < $15,750, so this test does not require a return. Other rules may still require one.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 1. 2025 Filing Requirements Chart for Most Taxpayers”, p. 2
notes.evidence: single under 65 $15,750 65 or older $17,750

notes.front: A single dependent under 65 and not blind must file for 2025 if unearned income was more than {{c1::$1,350}}.
notes.explanation: This is one of three separate triggers in Table 1-2; meeting any one of them means a return is required.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Table 1-2. 2025 Filing Requirements for Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Single dependents—Were you either age 65 or older or blind? No. You must file a return if any of the following apply. • Your unearned income was more than $1,350.

notes.front: A single dependent under 65 and not blind must file for 2025 if earned income was more than {{c1::$15,750}}.
notes.explanation: Earned income here means salaries, wages, tips, professional fees and taxable scholarship and fellowship grants.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Table 1-2. 2025 Filing Requirements for Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Your earned income was more than $15,750.

notes.front: A single dependent (under 65, not blind) must also file if gross income is more than the larger of which two amounts?
notes.back: $1,350, or earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.
notes.explanation: For this table, gross income is simply earned plus unearned income, so a mix of small amounts can still trigger a return.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Table 1-2. 2025 Filing Requirements for Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Your gross income was more than the larger of: • $1,350, or • Your earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.

notes.front: Lena, 17, single, not blind, is her parents’ dependent. In 2025 she earned $3,000 in wages and had $1,000 of taxable interest. Must she file?
notes.back: B: yes, $4,000 is more than $3,450.
notes.choices:
A) No: each type of income is under its own limit
B) Yes: her gross income is more than the larger of $1,350 or her earned income plus $450
C) No: dependents never file
notes.choicesExplained: B misses the third test, on combined gross income. C is wrong: Table 1-2 exists because dependents often must file.
notes.explanation: Step by step: unearned $1,000 ≤ $1,350 and earned $3,000 ≤ $15,750, so neither alone triggers a return. Gross income $3,000 + $1,000 = $4,000; larger of $1,350 or $3,000 + $450 = $3,450; $4,000 > $3,450, so she must file.
notes.source: Publication 17 (2025), Your Federal Income Tax, “Table 1-2. 2025 Filing Requirements for Dependents”, p. 11
notes.evidence: Your gross income was more than the larger of: • $1,350, or • Your earned income (up to $15,300) plus $450.

notes.front: On what day is marital status judged for filing status, and who counts as unmarried for the whole year?
notes.back: The last day of the tax year. You are unmarried if then unmarried, or legally separated under a divorce or separate maintenance decree.
notes.explanation: State law decides whether you are married or legally separated under such a decree.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Marital Status: Unmarried persons”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You are considered unmarried for the whole year if, on the last day of your tax year, you are either: • Unmarried, or • Legally separated from your spouse under a divorce or separate maintenance decree.

notes.front: A married couple cannot agree to file jointly. Which filing status must each spouse use, and what is the exception?
notes.back: Married filing separately, unless the spouse qualifies for head of household.
notes.explanation: A joint return needs both spouses’ agreement, so without it the default is a separate return.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Married Filing Separately”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you and your spouse don’t agree to file a joint return, you must use this filing status unless you qualify for head of household status, discussed later.

notes.front: Dana’s divorce decree became final on 30 December 2025. Is she married or unmarried for her 2025 filing status?
notes.back: A: unmarried for the whole of 2025.
notes.choices:
A) Unmarried for the whole of 2025
B) Married, because she was married for most of 2025
C) Married for 2025 and unmarried from 2026
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: marital status is tested on the last day of the tax year, not by how many months you were married.
notes.explanation: On 31 December 2025 Dana was unmarried, so Publication 501 treats her as unmarried for the whole year.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Marital Status: Unmarried persons”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You are considered unmarried for the whole year if, on the last day of your tax year, you are either: • Unmarried, or

notes.front: For head of household, what share of the cost of keeping up the home must you pay?
notes.back: More than half the cost of keeping up a home for the year.
notes.explanation: This is the second of the three head of household requirements, alongside being unmarried and having a qualifying person.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Head of Household”, p. 8
notes.evidence: 2. You paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for the year.

notes.front: For head of household, a qualifying person must live with you in the home for {{c1::more than half the year}}, apart from temporary absences such as school.
notes.back: More than half the year.
notes.explanation: Temporary absences, such as time away at school, still count as time living with you.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Head of Household”, p. 8
notes.evidence: 3. A qualifying person lived with you in the home for more than half the year (except for temporary absences, such as school).

notes.front: Which qualifying person does not have to live with you for head of household status?
notes.back: Your dependent parent.
notes.explanation: Publication 501 makes this an exception to the third requirement, that the qualifying person lived with you for more than half the year.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Head of Household”, p. 8
notes.evidence: However, if the qualifying person is your dependent parent, your dependent parent doesn’t have to live with you.

notes.front: Tomás has never married. He pays 70% of the costs of his home, where his 9-year-old daughter, his dependent, lived all of 2025. Which status fits best?
notes.back: C: head of household.
notes.choices:
A) Qualifying surviving spouse
B) Single
C) Head of household
notes.choicesExplained: B is available but ignores a status he meets, and the publication says to pick the lowest-tax one. C needs a spouse who died.
notes.explanation: Check each test: unmarried on 31 December; 70% is more than half the home’s cost; his daughter lived with him all year, which is more than half.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Head of Household”, p. 8
notes.evidence: You may be able to file as head of household if you meet all the following requirements. 1. You are unmarried or considered unmarried on the last day of the year.

notes.front: For qualifying surviving spouse, what must have been true about the year your spouse died?
notes.back: You were entitled to file a joint return with your spouse for that year, whether or not you actually did.
notes.explanation: Being entitled to a joint return is the test; the return actually filed that year does not matter.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse: Eligibility rules”, p. 10
notes.evidence: 1. You were entitled to file a joint return with your spouse for the year your spouse died. It doesn’t matter whether you actually filed a joint return.

notes.front: To file 2025 as qualifying surviving spouse, your spouse must have died in {{c1::2023 or 2024}} and you must not have remarried before the end of 2025.
notes.explanation: These are the 2 years following the year of death; for a 2025 death, the survivor can file jointly for 2025 if otherwise eligible.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse: Eligibility rules”, p. 11
notes.evidence: 2. Your spouse died in 2023 or 2024 and you didn’t remarry before the end of 2025.

notes.front: For qualifying surviving spouse, which child must you have, and which kind of child does not count?
notes.back: A child or stepchild you can (or could) claim as a dependent; a foster child does not count.
notes.explanation: “Could claim” covers a child you cannot claim only because of their own gross income, their joint return, or your being someone else’s dependent.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse: Eligibility rules”, p. 11
notes.evidence: 3. You have a child or stepchild (not a foster child) whom you can claim as a dependent or could claim as a dependent except that, for 2025: a. The child had gross income of $5,200 or more, b. The child filed a joint return, or c. You could be claimed as a dependent on someone else’s return.

notes.front: Ruth’s husband died in 2022. She has not remarried, and her dependent son lives with her. Can she file 2025 as qualifying surviving spouse?
notes.back: A: no, her 2 years were 2023 and 2024.
notes.choices:
A) No: the 2 years after a 2022 death are 2023 and 2024
B) Yes: she has not remarried
C) Yes: the status lasts while a dependent child lives with her
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: not remarrying and having a child are needed, but the status is limited to 2 years after the year of death.
notes.explanation: Step by step: death in 2022; the following 2 years are 2023 and 2024; 2025 is the third year, so the status is no longer available.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse”, p. 10
notes.evidence: You may be eligible to use qualifying surviving spouse as your filing status for 2 years following the year your spouse died.

notes.front: Qualifying child relationship test: which relatives pass it?
notes.back: Your child, stepchild, foster child, sibling, half- or step-sibling, or a descendant of any of them.
notes.explanation: Because descendants count, a niece, nephew or grandchild can pass this test.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 1. The child must be your son, daughter, stepchild, foster child, brother, sister, half brother, half sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, or a descendant of any of them.

notes.front: Qualifying child age test: what are the three ways to pass it?
notes.back: Under 19 at year end; under 24 at year end and a student; or any age if permanently and totally disabled.
notes.explanation: In the first two cases the child must also be younger than you, or than your spouse if filing jointly.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 2. The child must be (a) under age 19 at the end of the year and younger than you (or your spouse if filing jointly); (b) under age 24 at the end of the year, a student, and younger than you (or your spouse if filing jointly); or (c) any age if permanently and totally disabled.

notes.front: Qualifying child residency test: the child must have lived with you for {{c1::more than half of the year}}.
notes.back: More than half of the year.
notes.explanation: Publication 501 attaches exceptions to this test in a footnote, so check them before failing a child on residency.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 3. The child must have lived with you for more than half of the year.

notes.front: Qualifying child support test: whose support is measured, and what is the limit?
notes.back: The child’s own: the child must not have provided more than half of their own support for the year.
notes.explanation: The test looks at what the child paid, not at what you paid; the qualifying relative test works the other way.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 4. The child must not have provided more than half of the child’s own support for the year.

notes.front: Qualifying child joint return test: when does a child’s joint return not disqualify them?
notes.back: When the joint return is filed only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid.
notes.explanation: Otherwise a child filing a joint return for the year cannot be your qualifying child.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 5. The child must not be filing a joint return for the year (unless that joint return is filed only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid).

notes.front: Amir, 40, has a nephew aged 22 at the end of 2025, a full-time student, who lives with him all year and pays little of his own support. Does the nephew pass the age test?
notes.back: C: yes, he is under 24, a student and younger than Amir.
notes.choices:
A) No: a nephew can never be a qualifying child
B) No: he is 19 or older
C) Yes: under 24, a student and younger than Amir
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores the student rule, which extends the age limit to under 24. C is wrong: a nephew is a descendant of a sibling, which the relationship test allows.
notes.explanation: Step by step: 22 is not under 19, so rule (a) fails; 22 is under 24, he is a student and younger than 40-year-old Amir, so rule (b) is met.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Child”, p. 12
notes.evidence: (b) under age 24 at the end of the year, a student, and younger than you (or your spouse if filing jointly);

notes.front: Qualifying relative gross income test for 2025: the person’s gross income must be less than {{c1::$5,200}}.
notes.explanation: A qualifying child has no gross income test, which is one reason the two categories give different answers.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 3. The person’s gross income for the year must be less than $5,200

notes.front: Qualifying relative support test: who must provide the support, and how much?
notes.back: You must provide more than half of the person’s total support for the year.
notes.explanation: Contrast the qualifying child test, which asks only whether the child supported themselves.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 4. You must provide more than half of the person’s total support for the year.

notes.front: A person is not related to you in any listed way. How can they still pass the qualifying relative relationship test?
notes.back: By living with you all year as a member of your household, in a relationship that doesn’t violate local law.
notes.explanation: The test is either a listed relationship or all-year membership of your household; one is enough.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative”, p. 12
notes.evidence: must live with you all year as a member of your household2 (and your relationship must not violate local law).

notes.front: Grace pays 80% of her widowed mother’s support. Her mother, who lives alone, had $6,000 of taxable interest in 2025. Is her mother Grace’s qualifying relative?
notes.back: B: no, $6,000 fails the gross income test.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: Grace provides more than half her support
B) No: her gross income is not less than $5,200
C) Yes: parents never have a gross income test
notes.choicesExplained: B is true but not enough: every test must be passed. C is wrong: the gross income test applies to every qualifying relative.
notes.explanation: Step by step: support 80% > 50% passes; gross income $6,000 is not less than $5,200, so the gross income test fails.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 3. The person’s gross income for the year must be less than $5,200

notes.front: If you could be claimed as a dependent by another taxpayer, can you claim your own dependents?
notes.back: No, unless that taxpayer files only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid.
notes.explanation: The same bar applies if your spouse could be claimed and you file jointly.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Overview of the Rules for Claiming a Dependent”, p. 12
notes.evidence: You can’t claim any dependents if you, or your spouse if filing jointly, could be claimed as a dependent by another taxpayer, unless that taxpayer files a return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid.

notes.front: Which people can be claimed as a dependent under the citizen or resident test?
notes.back: A U.S. citizen, U.S. resident alien or U.S. national, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.
notes.explanation: A nonresident alien living outside Canada and Mexico fails this test.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Overview of the Rules for Claiming a Dependent”, p. 12
notes.evidence: You can’t claim a person as a dependent unless that person is a U.S. citizen, a U.S. resident alien, a U.S. national, or a resident of Canada or Mexico.

notes.front: A child is the qualifying child of a parent and of a non-parent. Under the tiebreaker rules, whose qualifying child is it?
notes.back: The parent’s.
notes.explanation: The parent rule applies when only one of the persons is the child’s parent.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Tiebreaker rules”, p. 15
notes.evidence: of the persons is the child’s parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent.

notes.front: Two parents who don’t file jointly both claim the same qualifying child. Whose child does the IRS treat it as?
notes.back: The parent the child lived with for the longer period during the year.
notes.explanation: Only if the child lived with each parent equally does the next rule, on adjusted gross income, decide.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Tiebreaker rules”, p. 15
notes.evidence: If the parents don’t file a joint return together but both parents claim the child as a qualifying child, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent with whom the child lived for the longer period of time during the year.

notes.front: Both parents claim the child, and the child lived with each for the same time. Which parent wins?
notes.back: The parent with the higher adjusted gross income (AGI) for the year.
notes.explanation: Time lived with the child is checked first; AGI only breaks an exact tie on time.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Tiebreaker rules”, p. 15
notes.evidence: If the child lived with each parent for the same amount of time, the IRS will treat the child as the qualifying child of the parent who had the higher AGI for the year.

notes.front: Nia (unmarried) and her daughter live with Nia’s mother all year. The child is a qualifying child of both. Nia’s AGI is $28,000; the grandmother’s is $60,000. Both claim her. Who wins?
notes.back: C: Nia, the parent.
notes.choices:
A) Whoever filed first
B) The grandmother, because her AGI is higher
C) Nia, because she is the parent
notes.choicesExplained: B applies the AGI rule, which is used only when no parent is involved or parents tie. C is not a tiebreaker rule.
notes.explanation: Only one of the two is the child’s parent, so the parent rule decides before any AGI comparison.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Tiebreaker rules”, p. 15
notes.evidence: of the persons is the child’s parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent.

notes.front: Elena became a lawful permanent resident in 2019. She spent most of 2025 abroad, but her status was never taken away or found abandoned. Is she a resident under the green card test for 2025?
notes.back: A: yes, her lawful permanent resident status continues.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: her status continues until taken away or found abandoned
B) No: she was not in the United States for 183 days
C) No: living abroad ends the status automatically
notes.choicesExplained: B applies the substantial presence test, which a green card holder does not need. C is wrong: the status ends only when taken away or found abandoned.
notes.explanation: She held lawful permanent resident status at some time in 2025, and nothing ended it, so the green card test is met.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Green Card Test”, p. 4
notes.evidence: You continue to have resident status under this test unless the status is taken away from you or is administratively or judicially determined to have been abandoned.

notes.front: To meet the substantial presence test for 2025, you must be physically present in the United States on at least {{c1::31}} days during 2025.
notes.back: 31 days.
notes.explanation: This is a separate minimum from the 183-day three-year total; failing it ends the test however many earlier days you had.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Substantial Presence Test”, p. 5
notes.evidence: 1. 31 days during 2025; and 2. 183 days during the 3-year period

notes.front: In the 183-day count of the substantial presence test for 2025, what fraction of 2024 and 2023 days do you count?
notes.back: All 2025 days, one-third of 2024 days and one-sixth of 2023 days.
notes.explanation: Weighting earlier years means long past stays count for less than recent ones.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Substantial Presence Test”, p. 5
notes.evidence: a. All the days you were present in 2025, b. 1/3 of the days you were present in 2024, and c. 1/6 of the days you were present in 2023.

notes.front: Kenji, no green card, was in the United States 150 days in 2025, 90 days in 2024 and 120 days in 2023. Does he meet the substantial presence test for 2025?
notes.back: B: yes, his weighted total is 200 days.
notes.choices:
A) No: 150 days is under 183
B) Yes: 150 + 30 + 20 = 200 days
C) No: he needs 183 days in each year
notes.choicesExplained: B forgets to add weighted days from 2024 and 2023. C misreads the test: 183 is a three-year weighted total, not a yearly figure.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Substantial Presence Test”, p. 5
notes.evidence: 2. 183 days during the 3-year period that includes 2025, 2024, and 2023, counting: a. All the days you were present in 2025, b. 1/3 of the days you were present in 2024, and c. 1/6 of the days you were present in 2023.

notes.front: Your client’s dependent mother is a resident alien who has no social security number and is not eligible for one. What must she do before she can be listed?
notes.back: A: apply for an ITIN on Form W-7.
notes.choices:
A) Apply for an ITIN using Form W-7
B) Apply for a social security number anyway
C) Nothing: she can be listed without a number
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she is not eligible for a social security number. C is wrong: Publication 501 says such a dependent must apply for an ITIN.
notes.explanation: The rule covers resident and nonresident alien dependents who have no social security number and cannot get one.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Taxpayer identification numbers for aliens”, p. 23
notes.evidence: If your dependent is a resident or nonresident alien who doesn’t have and isn’t eligible to get an SSN, your dependent must apply for an ITIN. For details on how to apply, see Form W-7, Application for IRS Individual Taxpayer Identification Number.

notes.front: What happens if an e-filed return leaves out an IP PIN the IRS issued to the taxpayer?
notes.back: The electronic signature is invalid and the return is rejected.
notes.explanation: All six digits must appear for the electronic signature to be complete.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Identity Protection PIN”, p. 66
notes.evidence: Failure to include an issued IP PIN on the electronic return will result in an invalid signature and a rejected return.

notes.front: How often are IP PINs issued, and which returns does the IP PIN sent in early 2026 cover?
notes.back: Every year. It is used on the 2025 return and on any prior-year returns filed in 2026.
notes.explanation: The new IP PINs are generally sent out by mid-January 2026.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Identity Protection PIN”, p. 66
notes.evidence: New IP PINs are generated every year. They will generally be CAUTION sent out by mid-January 2026. Use this IP PIN on your 2025 return as well as any prior-year returns you file in 2026.

notes.front: In 2026 you e-file a joint 2025 return. Both spouses were issued IP PINs. What do you enter?
notes.back: B: both IP PINs.
notes.choices:
A) Only the first-named spouse’s IP PIN
B) Both spouses’ IP PINs in the spaces provided
C) Neither: IP PINs are for paper returns only
notes.choicesExplained: B risks a rejected return, because every issued IP PIN must appear. C is wrong: the IP PIN completes the electronic signature.
notes.explanation: The instructions say to enter both IP PINs when both joint filers received one.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Identity Protection PIN”, p. 66
notes.evidence: If you are filing a joint return and both taxpayers were issued an IP PIN, enter both IP PINs in the spaces provided.

notes.front: When e-signing with a Self-Select PIN, when do you not need the prior-year AGI from last year’s return?
notes.back: When you use your prior-year PIN or enter your IP PIN.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the AGI from the originally filed 2024 return is needed, and a transcript is one way to get it.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Self-Select PIN”, p. 66
notes.evidence: If you use your prior-year PIN or enter your IP PIN, you are not required to enter your prior-year AGI.

notes.front: Under the Taxpayer Bill of Rights, what may taxpayers expect from IRS notices and correspondence?
notes.back: Clear explanations of the laws and IRS procedures, and of IRS decisions about their tax accounts.
notes.explanation: This is part of “The Right to Be Informed”, the first right in the Taxpayer Bill of Rights.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “The Taxpayer Bill of Rights: The Right to Be Informed”, p. 125
notes.evidence: They are entitled to clear explanations of the laws and IRS procedures in all tax forms, instructions, publications, notices, and correspondence. They have the right to be informed of IRS decisions about their tax accounts and to receive clear explanations of the outcomes.

notes.front: Ava, a single U.S. citizen aged 30, lives in Portugal. In 2025 she earned $20,000 there and nothing in the United States. Must her filing check use that income?
notes.back: B: yes, worldwide gross income is compared with the threshold.
notes.choices:
A) No: only U.S.-source income counts
B) Yes: the threshold is compared with her worldwide gross income
C) No: citizens abroad never file
notes.choicesExplained: B describes how nonresident aliens are taxed, not citizens. C is wrong: citizens abroad generally follow the same filing rules.
notes.explanation: Step by step: worldwide gross income $20,000; the single, under-65 threshold is $15,750; $20,000 is at least $15,750, so she generally must file.
notes.source: Publication 54 (Rev. December 2025), Tax Guide for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Abroad, “Filing Requirements”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Generally, you must file an income tax return for any year in which your worldwide gross income is at least the amount shown for your filing status

notes.front: For 2025, paying one household employee how much in cash wages sends you to Schedule H?
notes.back: $2,800 or more.
notes.explanation: Schedule H decides whether household employment taxes are owed; wages of a student under 18 are not counted.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Schedule 2, line 9: Household employment taxes”, p. 113
notes.evidence: You paid any one household employee (defined below) cash wages of $2,800 or more in 2025.

notes.front: A client had a foreign bank account and foreign financial assets in 2025. Which schedule part and which form may apply?
notes.back: Part III of Schedule B, and possibly Form 8938.
notes.explanation: Form 3520 may also apply if the client dealt with a foreign trust.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Foreign-Source Income: Foreign accounts and trusts; Foreign financial assets”, p. 23
notes.evidence: You must complete Part III of Schedule B if you: • Had a foreign account; or

notes.front: A joint refund may be offset against one spouse’s past-due debt. Which form lets the other spouse ask for their share back?
notes.back: Form 8379, Injured Spouse Allocation.
notes.explanation: The instructions say the other spouse’s part may be refunded if certain conditions apply.
notes.source: Instructions for Form 1040 and 1040-SR (2025), “Injured Spouse”, p. 62
notes.evidence: But your part of the overpayment may be refunded to you if certain conditions apply and you complete Form 8379.

notes.front: For disasters declared after July 24, 2025, which newly covered disasters can postpone deadlines such as filing and paying income tax?
notes.back: Qualified state-declared disasters.
notes.explanation: The Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act expanded the mandatory postponement beyond federal declarations.
notes.source: Publication 547 (2025), Casualties, Disasters, and Thefts, “What’s New: Expansion of mandatory postponement”, p. 1
notes.evidence: The Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act expanded the mandatory postponement of certain tax deadlines for disasters declared after July 24, 2025. Taxpayers affected by qualified state-declared disasters may now qualify for the postponement of certain tax deadlines such as filing or paying income, excise, and employment taxes;

notes.front: On the 2025 Form 8615, line 2, a child who did not itemize deductions enters {{c1::$2,700}}.
notes.explanation: Line 2 is subtracted from the child’s unearned income on line 1 to find net unearned income.
notes.source: Form 8615 (2025), Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income, “Part I, line 2”, p. 1
notes.evidence: If the child did not itemize deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040) or Schedule A (Form 1040-NR), enter $2,700.

notes.front: On Form 8615, what do you do if line 1 minus line 2 is zero or less?
notes.back: Stop: don’t complete the rest of the form, but still attach it to the child’s return.
notes.explanation: Zero or less means the child has no net unearned income for the form to tax.
notes.source: Form 8615 (2025), Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income, “Part I, line 3”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Subtract line 2 from line 1. If zero or less, stop; do not complete the rest of this form but do attach it to the child’s return

notes.front: Priya, 12, had $4,000 of unearned income in 2025 and did not itemize. What is her net unearned income on Form 8615, line 3?
notes.choicesExplained: B skips the $2,700 subtraction on line 2. C would apply only if unearned income were $2,700 or less.
notes.explanation: Step by step: line 1 $4,000; line 2 $2,700 (no itemizing); line 3 = $4,000 − $2,700 = $1,300.
notes.source: Form 8615 (2025), Tax for Certain Children Who Have Unearned Income, “Part I, lines 1–3”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Enter the child’s unearned income. See instructions . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . If the child did not itemize deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040) or Schedule A (Form 1040-NR), enter $2,700.

notes.front: For the premium tax credit, what is your family size?
notes.back: The number of qualifying individuals in your tax family, including yourself.
notes.explanation: Publication 974 adds that listing a dependent by name and SSN or ITIN on the return is the same as claiming them as a dependent.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit (PTC), “Terms you may need to know: Family size”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Your family size equals the number of qualifying individuals in your tax family (including yourself). Note: Listing your dependents by name and social security number (SSN) or individual taxpayer identification number (ITIN) on your tax return is the same as claiming them as a dependent.

notes.front: For the premium tax credit, what household income, compared with the federal poverty line for your family size, is generally required?
notes.back: At least 100% of the federal poverty line for your family size.
notes.explanation: Income below 100% does not disqualify you if you meet the requirements set out under Line 5 of the Form 8962 instructions.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit (PTC), “Who Can Take the PTC”, p. 4
notes.evidence: Your household income for 2025 is at least 100% of the federal poverty line for your family size

notes.front: A couple filing jointly have modified AGIs of $50,000 and $20,000. Their dependent son, 16, earned $3,000 in wages and was not required to file. What is their household income?
notes.choicesExplained: B adds the son’s income, but only dependents required to file are included. C leaves out the spouse on a joint return.
notes.explanation: Step by step: $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000 for the couple; the son was not required to file, so his $3,000 is not added.
notes.source: Publication 974 (2025), Premium Tax Credit (PTC), “Household income”, p. 4
notes.evidence: plus the modified AGI of each individual whom you claim as a dependent and who is required to file an income tax return because their income meets the income tax return filing threshold

notes.front: Both spouses have income. How does Publication 501 suggest choosing between married filing jointly and married filing separately?
notes.back: Figure the tax both ways and choose the lower combined tax, unless you are required to file separately.
notes.explanation: A joint return may give lower tax, but not always; comparing both is the only way to know.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Married Filing Jointly”, p. 6
notes.evidence: come, you may want to figure your tax both on a joint return and on separate returns (using the filing status of married filing separately). You can choose the method that gives the two of you the lower combined tax unless you are required to file separately.

notes.front: A married person living apart from their spouse qualifies for head of household. What might HOH give them over married filing separately?
notes.back: Possibly lower tax, access to certain tax benefits, and a higher standard deduction.
notes.explanation: Publication 501 lists these when someone considered unmarried can file as HOH instead of MFS.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Married Filing Separately”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you qualify to file as head of household, instead of as married filing separately, your tax may be lower, you may be able to claim certain tax benefits, and your standard deduction will be higher.

notes.front: What does the qualifying surviving spouse status give, and what does it not give, compared with a joint return?
notes.back: It gives joint return tax rates and the highest standard deduction, but not the right to file a joint return.
notes.explanation: The survivor still files their own return; the status only borrows the joint rates.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Qualifying Surviving Spouse”, p. 10
notes.evidence: This filing status entitles you to use joint return tax rates and the highest standard deduction amount (if you don’t itemize deductions). It doesn’t entitle you to file a joint return.

notes.front: How does the income taxed differ for a resident alien and a nonresident alien?
notes.back: Resident aliens: generally worldwide income, like citizens. Nonresident aliens: only U.S.-source income and certain U.S. business income.
notes.explanation: Nonresident aliens are also taxed on certain income connected with a U.S. trade or business, not only on U.S.-source income.
notes.source: Publication 519 (2025), U.S. Tax Guide for Aliens, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.evidence: Resident aliens are generally taxed on their worldwide income, the same as U.S. citizens. Nonresident aliens are taxed only on their income from sources within the United States and on certain income connected with the conduct of a trade or business in the United States.

notes.front: Can someone who is the qualifying child of another taxpayer be your qualifying relative?
notes.back: No. A qualifying relative can’t be your qualifying child or anyone else’s.
notes.explanation: The test looks at every taxpayer, not just you: a child who qualifies for someone else is ruled out too.
notes.source: Publication 501 (2025), Dependents, Standard Deduction, and Filing Information, “Table 5. Tests To Be a Qualifying Relative”, p. 12
notes.evidence: 1. The person can’t be your qualifying child or the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
